title: Tavi and Cora's Highland Rescue
markdown:
Tavi was an apprentice falcon trainer, and a right good one too. He had a gift, a real knack for understanding those magnificent sharp-eyed birds. He could read their every twitch, their every keen glance. But the training manuals never mentioned the secret that made his knees knock and his tummy flip. Tavi was absolutely, positively terrified of heights. It made training the high-flying kestrels a jiggly business, full of deep breaths and the hope that he would not drop his whistle. It was a peculiar problem for a boy who was supposed to be a master of the skies.

His companion on the adventure that would test him was Cora, the miller’s niece. Cora was not content with the scent of flour and the rumble of the grindstones. She had eyes like a hawk herself, always spotting the tiniest detail — a loose pebble, a hidden cluster of wild strawberries, a tell-tale smudge of jam on a baker’s cheek from three stalls away. Her mind worked like a perfectly oiled mill wheel, grinding out solutions faster than you could say flour power. She saw the world in intricate patterns, always connecting the dots. If a cave mouth hid behind a shift in the rock, Cora would have seen it first.

The highlands were a place of swirling mist and ancient mystery, where paths twisted like mischievous ribbons and the wind liked to play tag with your hat, your cloak, and sometimes your sense of direction. Two important search parties, full of sturdy folk and keen trackers, had gone missing there, swallowed by thick disorienting fog and the bumbling confusion of the landscape. Master Borin, Tavi’s stern eagle-faced falcon master, a man who rarely smiled but whose approval was worth more than a king’s ransom, declared with a voice like thunder, “Tavi. You and Cora. Find them. Now. And no dawdling.” Tavi’s stomach did a triple somersault, mostly from the chilling thought of the sheer cliffs he would have to face.

“Hawk Country, you say?” Cora mused, adjusting her spectacles that always seemed to magnify her already keen vision. “That’s where the wind is so strong it can carry a giggle right out of your throat and leave you speechless. I’ve heard the echoes there can play tricks on your ears, making you think whispers are shouts, or that the rustle of leaves is a hungry beast.”

“And the Broken Ravines,” Tavi mumbled, feeling a cold dread creep up his spine. “They say the rocks there look like dragon teeth gnawing at the sky. And the paths disappear like smoke. You could blink and miss them, and then you’d be in quite a pickle.”

They set off, Tavi clutching his polished training whistle like a lifeline to solid ground, Cora practically skipping with an explorer’s zeal. The path, at first, was deceptively gentle, winding through whispering pines and meadows that smelled of wild thyme and damp cool earth. A kestrel hung high above them, a dark comma on the pale sky, and Tavi made himself watch it until his neck ached. If the bird could hang there, he told himself, he could walk a little farther. But soon the path led them straight into the heart of Hawk Country. The wind howled, a playful but powerful entity, tugging at their cloaks and trying to steal their hats. Tavi froze, his boots suddenly glued to the ground as if they had sprouted roots. His hands felt clammy, and his heart hammered a frantic drum solo against his ribs. He squeezed his eyes shut, the world spinning without his consent. “I can’t,” he whispered, the words barely audible above the gale. It felt like being a tiny boat tossed on a furious sea.

Cora, ever observant, grabbed his arm gently. “Tavi. Look.” She pointed not to the vast intimidating sky, but to something incredibly small and brave. A tiny impossibly bright blue butterfly was fluttering against the wind, its delicate wings working with remarkable strength and steady rhythm. “It’s not fighting the wind, Tavi,” she explained, her voice calm and clear. “It’s using it. See how its wings angle? It’s dancing with the currents.” Tavi dared to open one eye, then the other. The butterfly, a fragile speck of vibrant colour, danced in the gale, utterly unfazed. He took a deep shaky breath. He focused on the butterfly, on its determined flight. He took a wobbly step, his muscles screaming in protest. Then another. He was not flying, not by a long shot, but he was moving forward, defying the wind’s pull. He felt a tiny spark of courage ignite within him, like finding a hidden compass in his own heart.

The mist began to roll in then, thicker than Aunt Mildred’s notoriously lumpy pea soup, muffling sounds and blurring the landscape into an indistinguishable grey. The air grew cold and damp, carrying the faint earthy smell of wet rock, and a sudden gust of wind whispered past Tavi’s ear, raising goosebumps on his skin. Soon they found themselves teetering on the edge of the Broken Ravines. The ground here did not just crumble. It split and yawned open, sheer dizzying drops on either side, revealing the emptiness below. Tavi’s breath hitched. His knees wobbled like jelly on a particularly wobbly table at a village fête. His vision swam, and he felt himself swaying, even though he was still standing still. “No. Absolutely not,” he said, his voice strained.

“Hold on,” Cora said, her voice a steady anchor. She pointed not to a bridge of solid stone, but to a narrow moss-covered log that precariously bridged a dizzying chasm. Tavi’s stomach lurched. “Look closer,” Cora urged, her voice firm but reassuring. “See these tiny little moss patches clinging to the sides of the ravine? They grip the rock like tiny determined fingers. And if you look closely, just there,” she pointed to a section of the sheer rock face, “there are ancient carvings, faint etchings almost hidden by time. They’re small handholds. It’s like a ladder, but built sideways into the cliff.” She demonstrated with astonishing grace, her movements sure and steady as she tested each grip and foothold. “It’s not a sheer drop if you use the steps, Tavi. It’s a climb.”

He watched her, a flicker of something other than paralyzing fear igniting within him. It was determination, perhaps, or the dawning realization that he was not alone. He looked at the moss, at the faint etchings that were indeed there, begging to be discovered. He thought of the determined butterfly dancing in the wind. He took another deep breath, this one steadier, stronger. He copied Cora, placing his hand on the cool damp rock, feeling the rough texture beneath his fingertips. He felt a small grip, solid and promising. He tested it. It held. Slowly, painstakingly, his eyes fixed on Cora’s determined back, he followed her path. He moved, not by being fearless, but by being determined despite his fear. Each tiny movement was a victory. He reached the other side, his legs feeling like overcooked spaghetti, but his heart thrumming with a new kind of power, a quiet triumph. He had done it. He had actually, impossibly, done it.

Just then, as if conjured by their success, they heard voices. Distant shouts, confused and muffled by the swirling mist. “Which way did they go?” “I can’t see a thing.” The two search parties were close, so agonizingly close, but hopelessly lost to each other, their calls echoing with growing desperation. The wind was picking up speed, a low mournful moan that promised a fierce storm was rapidly rolling in.

Cora’s eyes lit up, a flash of inspiration like lightning in the gloom. “The wind. Tavi, your whistle. When Master Borin trains the falcons, what’s the signal for all clear, when everything is safe and sound?”

Tavi’s mind, now sharp and focused, flashed back to hours of patient practice. “A high, clear, trilling note,” he recalled, “followed by two short, sharp blasts.”

Cora grinned, a brilliant dazzling thing that cut through the mist like sunshine. “Perfect. Now, which way are the voices coming from?” She pointed left, then right, her finger tracing the faint sounds. “They’re split. We need to guide them together. Tavi, you take this side. I’ll take that. When you hear my signal, reply. Then send the all-clear call into the wind, loud and clear.”

Tavi nodded, his earlier terror now a distant memory, replaced by a surge of purpose. He raised his whistle and blew, a clear bright sound that cut through the mist like a beacon. Cora blew hers, a slightly different pitch, a melodic echo. They could hear the confused calls of the search parties getting closer, their urgency palpable. Then Tavi heard Cora’s whistle again, followed by a sharp clear blast from the direction she had indicated. He knew the second party was close to her, responding.

He took a deep breath, remembering the determined butterfly, remembering the challenging climb of the ravine. The mist tasted of wet stone. He set his boots wide, the way Master Borin had taught him to stand when a bird came in too fast, and he blew the high trilling note, then the two sharp decisive blasts. The sound leapt away from him and came back thinner, then stronger, as if the highland itself had decided to answer. He waited, his heart pounding, but this time it was with exhilarating anticipation, not debilitating dread.

A moment later, shouts of relief, joyous and unburdened, echoed through the highlands, stronger and clearer now. “Over there.” “I see them.” The mist parted just enough to reveal the two lost groups stumbling towards each other, arms outstretched in happy reunion. They were saved.

As the first fat drops of rain began to fall, a gentle patter at first, then growing bolder, Tavi looked at Cora, a wide beaming smile stretching across his face. He had not conquered his fear of heights, not entirely. But he had faced it, walked through it, and found his way out, stronger and wiser. And he had helped bring two lost groups home. That, he realized with a warmth spreading through his chest, was even braver than soaring with the mightiest falcon. He felt ten feet tall, and he was standing firmly, wonderfully, on the ground.
